speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a time of extraordinary events.
We see the government being ready to use unprecedented means in order to force a tax, the GST, which is the most unpopular tax in Canadian history, through Parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It seems to me that is debate.
We may be in extraordinary times, and those who were listening carefully to the prayer would notice that I had noticed that. Certainly, I will hear the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is using extraordinary means to force through Parliament the most unpopular tax in Canadian history, the goods and services tax.
Therefore, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to present immediately a motion as follows:
That this House direct the Prime Minister to take the steps
necessary for the Governor in Council to appoint a person who will
respect the rules of Parliament to preside over the Senate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reinforcing this motion, and in speaking to the motion, I would like to call on the British North America Act, section 34, which makes it very clear that the responsibility for naming the person in the Senate who becomes Speaker rests with section 34.
The Governor General may, from time to time-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am going to try to be as even-handed as I can.
A few days ago, the government rose to put forward a motion and asked for the consent of the House. There was some debate, I think 16 minutes on behalf of the government side and I think 13 minutes on behalf of the opposition side. I may have been too lax in indulging and giving everybody the latitude that was engaged in at the time.
Now before the House, there is a request by way of point of order by the hon. Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition that the House accept the motion which the hon. Leader of the Opposition has put forward on the basis of unanimous consent.
I recognized the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, but I think again we have to keep in mind that what the opposition is seeking here is exactly what the government was seeking the other day. That was unanimous consent for a motion.
My difficulty in dealing with this-I am sure all hon. members can understand this- is that it is legitimate enough, but it cannot be turned into a prolonged or extended debate.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition has put the point, and he has put it with his usual forcefulness. I am just wondering: Is there any particular need for other members to become involved? I know that the hon. parliamentary secretary is seeking the floor on a point of order, and I anticipate that he will be asking the same questions that I am putting in general terms to the House.
Probably the better way to deal with this would be to say that there is the motion. Perhaps I should ask if the House is prepared to agree to it or otherwise. However, I have some regard for our hon. friend, the member for Ottawa-Vanier. If he can persuade me that, as your Speaker, I should hear further debate, I may be persuaded. I am pointing out that the procedure that is being followed has been done many times in the House. Somebody has risen and asked for unanimous consent on a point of order. That is exactly what is happening. It is not appropriate for me to allow it to extend into a long debate.

Points of Order
Perhaps the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, who I interrupted, can assist the Chair, but not to debate what is or is not going on in some other place. I have some doubts as to whether that would be appropriate. I will hear the hon. member in order to decide whether I ought to hear the hon. member further.
The hon. parliamentary secretary on a point of order.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand very clearly your need to treat both sides fairly and we on this side appreciate and respect that principle. Keeping that in mind, the other day as the Speaker reminded us-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think there is any secret that we have been witnessing extraordinary events. Some of what has happened in the last 24 hours has never happened before. As your Speaker, I have to try to find a way to allow the House to deal with it, but still stay within the bounds of reason and within the rules. I am prepared to be very careful about making sure that we do both of those things and I certainly think that it is appropriate to allow the hon. parliamentary secretary to give his remarks to the House.
It seems to me that, given the backdrop of what we are dealing with, we ought to be very careful this morning. Let us listen to each other and see if we can find a way through it.
I will hear the hon. parliamentary secretary shortly, and I remind him that his point of order interrupts the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier. I will come back to the hon. member.
The hon. parliamentary secretary who may be able to help me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a couple of quick points.
First, you referred to the 16 minutes and the 13 minutes the other day which would lead us to believe that the opposition should have three minutes. However, yesterday, if my memory serves me right, the opposition took 32 minutes, so we should have 27 minutes.
I do want to say on the basis of the motion that the normal way for us to do this is to discuss it in House leader's meetings. We would be happy to do that. But without those discussions at this point, we would have to signal that, no, we will not give unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. parliamentary secretary has given clear indication that the House is not going to agree to the motion. The hon. parliamentary secretary has also, however, left the door open for some discussion. However, I am listening to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, and I will hear him to see if what he has to say is going to help the Speaker deal with this problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and appreciate your comments. Indeed, the Speaker is invested with powers to maintain order and I take exception to the government trying to bootleg some phoney points of order when I have the floor legitimately. I do not agree with this attitude that there has to be a quid pro quo, just because they get a few minutes we do not get as much.
The point is that the government is responsible for the appointments of certain persons. It is done by appointment, by Order in Council. The Governor General follows up on the recommendation. We all know that. The point of the motion is to get the government to put forward an appointment of a person who will, like you, Mr. Speaker, have respect for the rules of the House of Commons and have respect for the rules of Parliament. That is our point.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will hear the hon. member for Kamloops. I know that he will assist the Chair in not straying too far, given the situation.
I want to join with you, Mr. Speaker, and acknowledge as I am sure we all do that we have been witnessing some extraordinary events in the last 24 hours and it has demonstrated a whole number of very serious problems we face as a Parliament.
I simply want to say, Mr. Speaker, and I suspect I reflect the views of all of us on both sides of the House-perhaps we could call it a three-sided House- that while we might have different views on the other place in terms of its validity, we do recognize that the Parliament of Canada includes two Houses, that the work that is done here eventually moves into the other place and is concluded there, under normal conditions.
October 5, 1990

What we see this morning is that while we are here in our places to carry on important business, particularly as it refers to heritage languages in the country, we know full well that the other place is paralysed. It is non-functioning. It is not working.
While I sympathize with the point raised by my hon. friend, the Leader of the Official Opposition, I think what we have witnessed in the last few hours in the other place was a complete debacle or chaos, I think is a good way to describe it. If there ever has been a demonstration of the need to abolish the Senate, it has to be now.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kamloops has, I think, commented on events of which we are all very much aware. The hon. member has a certain minimum awareness of those events, as we all know, but this is not the place or the time to debate great constitutional changes.
I think that the appropriate thing is for me to put to the House the motion that has been proposed to us on the basis of asking consent that this House direct the Prime Minister to take the steps necessary for the Governor in Council to appoint a person who will respect the rules of Parliament and to preside over the Senate. That is the motion. Is there agreement to the motion?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have only heard the motion now twice, but it seems to me that some of the language in there would cause that motion to be ruled out of order because it sounds to me like a reflection on present occupants in the other House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. parliamentary secretary may well be right. At the moment, I am asking the House whether there is consent.
Agreed.
No.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are two motions in amendment in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East as set down in the Notice Paper for the report stage of Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute. Motion No. 1 is in order. A similar motion was moved in committee and negatived. However, Motion No. 1 is sufficiently different that the Chair is prepared to allow it to be put before the House.

Consequently, motion No. 1 will be debated and voted on separately.

Motion No. 2 is in order and it will also be debated and voted on separately.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-37 be amended in Clause 2 by striking out lines 16 and 17 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"Canada and does not include aboriginal languages of Canada."
She said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to just explain a little bit about this motion, though I know members of the committee will be well aware of why we felt it necessary to be very explicit that aboriginal people do not want to have their languages, the languages of the First Nations of Canada classified as heritage languages and included in this bill.
I know that in committee we did delete the section that was originally in the bill which included "and includes any aboriginal language" after the phrase "contributes to the linguistic heritage of Canada". However, having deleted that, in the view of a number of native people we heard from and to whom I have spoken since, it does not make explicit what their intention is, so we have added the phrase "and does not include aboriginal languages of Canada", so that there will be absolutely no mistake about this.
I would like to quote just a couple of things from two of the senior native groups that appeared before the committee or have written to us on this subject. Originally, the Assembly of First Nations did ask for a deletion of the phrase, which we responded to in committee, but they subsequently did ask for a more specific exclusion. Mr. Erasmus says, in his letter to members of Parliament:
Although we understand Aboriginal languages are not excluded from the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act, First Nations do not wish to be included in the definition of "Heritage Languages" in Bill C-37.
That is a letter dated dated last June, so it is referring to the original bill, before it was amended in committee. The letter goes on:

We are the "founding" languages of Canada,-
I think that is extremely important, not "heritage" languages but "founding" languages of Canada-
-and given the precarious future of our endangered languages, require a separate Aboriginal Languages Foundation/Institute.
He goes on to quote from the presentation that he made, in committee that, and I quote:
The First Nation's position that any federal policies or actions which impact upon Aboriginal people must ensure the recognition and affirmation of existing Aboriginal and treaty rights was reaffirmed in the Supreme Court of Canada -on the Sparrow case-in 1990. It is our submission that Aboriginal and treaty rights to language is with section 35 of the Constitution Act of Canada, 1981. Further, the federal government is obligated to consult with Indians-
This was not done, prior to this bill being drafted.
- in the development of legislation that directly impact our lives and must prove that any involvement of legislation will enhance the Indian position for protection.
They said that they did not believe that this proposed legislation would enhance their languages and wanted to be excluded. They also asked that we support an aboriginal languages foundation. I think that this is another thing that we must not forget. It is very important. I know my colleague will be speaking on that question in a little more detail.
Finally, I would like to mention as well on the question of aboriginal languages, a statement by Phil Fontaine, the provincial leader of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs. This was interestingly enough to the people of Quebec after the Meech Lake Accord was in effect turned down. He said that they supported Quebec's passionate dedication to the preservation and promotion of the French language and culture in Canada. He said: "We also are fighting for our culture and language. We, the aboriginal people of this country, have inherited through the oral traditions of our forbears, 55 different, distinct, original languages, 52 of these original languages of Canada are now on the brink of extinction. Unlike you, we cannot retrieve these languages from our mother country. Our mother country is Canada. What we lose in Canada, we lose forever". I think that very eloquently explains why the languages of founding peoples, which are founding languages of Canada and unique to Canada and North America, must be pre-
Govemment Orders
served in a separate way and much more strongly through an aboriginal language foundation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturaiism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly share the concern of the member for the preservation of aboriginal languages. I, too, am very disturbed by what appears to be a rather impossible situation where we have not been able, through the generations, to put forward a mechanism to guarantee the preservation of this important heritage, the languages and cultures of our founding peoples, our first peoples. This is not the issue which we are discussing today. As a matter of fact, there have been at least two excellent studies that I have had the opportunity of perusing personally. I have had lengthy discussions with the member of Parliament from Alberta. I think it was the member for Wetaskiwin. He and I are both pursuing the initiative very diligently.
However, the bill that we have before us is really the follow-up to the original Bill C-152 which was before the previous House. At that time members of both opposition parties, in particular the member for York West and Mr. Epp who was the critic-and, by the way, he did an excellent job on behalf of his party in all of the issues before us-explicitly brought forward the suggestion that aboriginal languages should be included. They had a concern that if they were not explicitly written into the bill there would be a very narrow and restrictive use of the institute, perhaps, and all aboriginal languages would not have access to any of the funding or the resources or the shared expertise that may become available by this institute and would be of great benefit in preserving heritage languages and cultures in Canada.
Certainly it was on reflection and having accepted the helpful suggestion of members of the opposition that when we brought forth Bill C-37 it was included. It was not in any way to abdicate or deny the responsibility for establishing an important process for the preservation of aboriginal languages. All of us, this summer, have certainly become much more aware of the unfairness, the inequalities, and the difficult situation that our first peoples found themselves in. There is a much greater commitment by all of us today to do everything we can to

October 5, 1990
Government Orders
restore equality, to give full participation, and to provide the same opportunity that all other Canadians have.
Today, however, I cannot accept the premise that the member has brought forward. Her proposal would have the effect of limiting and restricting the activities of the institute. I would not want to preclude instances where the aboriginal languages and cultures could participate actively. It is on these bases that I do not accept the suggestion of the member. Certainly the mere fact that it is not mentioned would have a tendency to give people the feeling that it is not there, but as far as I am concerned all languages and cultures must be preserved and protected.
It will be up to the people who will run the institute- the board of directors, administrative people, and the community from coast to coast-to decide how those resources will be used. I do not think it is up to us necessarily to restrict or narrow the opportunities this excellent institution will have.

Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment. I regret the fact that the hon. Secretary of State has decided not to support the amendment. After all, this amendment comes at the request of the aboriginal people of Canada through their representative organizations. This is not a request that was developed within the caucuses of a particular political party on the Hill. This request comes at the request of representative organizations of the aboriginal people.
If the Secretary of State would read the decision in the Sparrow case, he would find that as part of Canada's fiduciary obligations he has an obligation to consult with aboriginal people before bringing down legislation which deals with something as critical as their cultural survival and with languages which are key to cultural survival. This amendment is not coming at the request of a particular political party. It is coming at the request of the aboriginal people of Canada.
This minister in particular should respect the wishes of the aboriginal people of Canada who have made their views known in committee and to the various members of the House of Commons. It would be a shameful act if we did not consider these views, especially in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in the Sparrow case which calls upon the government, in recognition of its requirement for honour in dealing with the aboriginal people, to consult with the aboriginal people before
legislative changes are made. The wishes of the aboriginal people should be followed in this case.
The survival of aboriginal languages in this country, as my colleague has mentioned, is a fundamentally different issue from the survival of other, what we like to call, heritage languages. If you are of Spanish descent in Canada and you feel that your language is being threatened or that you have lost contact with your mother tongue, that language will survive in Europe or in Latin America or elsewhere in the world. If you are of Ukrainian descent or German descent, the same thing applies. If you are like me and you are descended from one of the Gaelic speaking groups, that language is dying out elsewhere in the world, but there are organizations in the mother countries that are attempting to protect and to save those languages. Action is even being taken here in Canada, Cape Breton, and elsewhere to protect those languages.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East, the fact is that if aboriginal languages die out, there is no other country. There is no other place in the world where these languages can be nurtured, incubated, and protected so that people can learn them again in this country. The mother country for those languages is right here in Canada, and it is here we have to take steps to protect them.
Aboriginal people do not want to have their languages, because of this fundamental difference, included among a whole group of heritage languages. The threats to aboriginal languages are fundamentally different. As my colleague has pointed out in a letter from the Assembly of First Nations, only three of the 53 aboriginal languages in Canada are likely to survive into the next century. That is less than 10 years from today. It is important that we as members of Parliament, in respect of our fiduciary responsibilities to the aboriginal people of this country, act immediately and take steps to make sure that those aboriginal languages are protected.
It seems that the minister is operating on the principle which applies to aboriginal people in Canada, that is, first here last served. This principle has to be reversed in the case of aboriginal people. It would have been important for the Secretary of State to stand up and accept this motion and at the same time make a positive statement to the aboriginal people of Canada, first, that he will consult with them on the formation of an aboriginal languages foundation to protect aboriginal
October 5, 1990

languages and to promote aboriginal languages in the country.
Second, he should have stood up and in a positive way have said that he would support the bill presented to this House in the name of the hon. member for Western Arctic, Bill C-269. He should have said that he would consult with the member who proposed that bill, with the aboriginal groups in Canada who support the bill, and with our caucus which supports the bill. He should have said that he would make sure the heritage languages legislation goes through the House and that Bill C-269 goes through at exactly the same time, and with appropriate funding, so that we can make sure these languages do survive into the 20th century because they are fundamental to the survival of aboriginal culture in this country.
We as a Parliament and members opposite as a government have an obligation spelled out in the Sparrow case and spelled out in our fiduciary responsibility to the native people in Canada to get that kind of legislation through as quickly as possible. It is shameful that a heritage language bill is going to go through this House first, before we have dealt with the founding languages of Canada.
I support both bills, but I think that the government should abandon its principle of first here, last served. We should consider the bill that has been presented to this House in the name of the member for Western Arctic, Bill C-269. That bill should be passed first and then we should pass Bill C-37.

Madam Speaker, I commend my colleague from Vancouver on her amendment that Bill C-37 not include aboriginal languages of Canada. I whole-heartedly support this amendment in that all of my life's work prior to coming to the House of Commons has been related to education or the enhancement and revitalization of aboriginal cultures and languages.
I must say that coming to the House of Commons has given me a forum in which I can express politically the views of the aboriginal people as they have been presented to me, because I come from an area that is
Government Orders
majority aboriginal and where the aboriginal languages have been deemed official.
In the past, under Secretary of State Serge Joyal, P.C., we negotiated in the Northwest Territories a $16 million aboriginal language agreement with the federal government. This funding will come to an end this year, I believe.
My question to the minister in the body of my speech concerns whether unspent moneys will be reprofiled and whether there will be an extension of this particular funding. This has specific reference to this amendment because aboriginal languages are not specific to a debate in the House of Commons. They relate to the concerns of the over-all aboriginal community. In an area that is predominantly aboriginal, I have to say, it is very important that these people have some kind of feeling as to whether or not their work is going to be able to continue.
There have been some very major steps taken. Anyone who knows the justice system in Canada will appreciate that in an area such as where I come from there are many people who are unilingual. Being served in a non-native milieu or in a non-native environment is sometimes very detrimental in applying the principles of social justice in the courts of law.
The territorial government has amended the Jury Act. To its credit I say that it has amended the Jury Act to include unilingual speaking members. They can now sit on a jury. That is quite profound in that the unilingual speaking members are aboriginal people.
I must say also that I share similar concerns as my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, the critic for aboriginal affairs. I have to say that he is quite right. I will take no credit for the basis on which my private members' bill, Bill C-269, an act to establish an aboriginal language foundation, was developed.
That work should be attributed to people like Mary Jamieson and other people from the Assembly of First Nations. However, I did sit on a policy development committee in 1986 and 1987 to assist them in developing a policy for the establishment of this foundation. It was the good will of Mr. Crombie that allowed this to happen.
I must say that there should be no limits set on the amount of money that it will take to preserve the 53

October 5, 1990
Government Orders
aboriginal languages. If I might, I would just like to say the following in my aboriginal language. That was my first language, taught to me by my grandmother.
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Dene-North Slavey. ] [English]
What I have said, Madam Speaker, is that the essence of aboriginal languages is who you are specifically, culturally, and your heart and your mind are spoken through your language. Our language is a living language. It is a language that expresses our psychology. If our languages die or are not able to flourish because we do not have the mechanisms to revitalize them or to enhance them, then the will and the culture of the people die, the spirit of the people dies.
We come from an oral tradition, Madam Speaker. This oral tradition is one that has been carried on for thousands of generations. Does it not amaze Canadians that a member of Parliament can rise in the House of Commons and speak Inuktituk as can my hon. colleague the hon. member for Nunatsiaq, and Cree as can my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. It is quite amazing that I can rise and speak in my aboriginal language when those were basically unwritten languages. They have been passed on for thousands of generations from our forefathers. It is a gift, a very special gift, and in order to keep that gift I make this appeal to the government.
Please give unanimous consent for Bill C-269, not to give me profile but to honour the needs expressed by the aboriginal community. They want an aboriginal language foundation because if there isn't one there are only three languages that can survive, Cree, Ojibway, and Inuktituk.
Madam Speaker, may I say to you that our battle has not just been on this front, not just for resources specifically, but constitutionally. I fought hard to get a clause in the Meech Lake Accord that expressed the will of my people concerning their linguistic and cultural rights. It was denied. We worked very hard in the Charest committee to entrench these in the Constitution.
I cannot believe that we can achieve a constitutional balance in Canada with other groups until the government has defined its relationship with the first people. There will never be the kind of constitutional balance that this country needs because it is inherently wrong to
exclude the first nations in terms of their languages and their cultures. That is who they are.
Madam Speaker, may I end by saying this to you. If we do establish an aboriginal language foundation, it would be to the credit of the government, to the credit of the various individuals that were involved in doing all of the research and all of the work along with the Assembly of First Nations. It could be a co-operative approach.
Why did the House leader not respond positively when I wrote to him? He applauded in great glowing terms what I was trying to achieve with Bill C-269, the act to establish an aboriginal language foundation, but would not give consent. I cannot understand how that fundamental right, to be able to speak in your first language, can be denied by any government.

Madam Speaker, I do wish to say a few words on this amendment to the act to establish a heritage language institute.
I want to begin by saying that during the last three or four months I have had a very remarkable flow of unsolicited comments to my offices in Ttinity-Spadina and on the Hill here, in writing and in telephone calls, expressing almost unanimous support for the general cause of Canada's first nations. Most of comments did not speak specifically about this or that issue, although they were stimulated by the controversy around Kanesa-take. They simply asserted a general feeling that the first nations have not had a fair deal and that we have to act now to change that situation.
It is in that context that I want to speak about the amendment of my colleague, the member for Vancouver East, which would insert the words "that the heritage language institute mandate does not include aboriginal languages of Canada".
As has been pointed out, this proposal did not originate with the caucus of which I am a member. This proposal originated with a group such as the Assembly of First Nations. This is their request. I wish that the government would give it more careful consideration than it appears to have done.
I am not an expert on the subject of aboriginal affairs. My wife, Alice, did live for four years at the place she learned to call Caughnawaga. We now understand that its name is Kahnawake or something close to that. Her father was the United Church missionary there and she and her young sisters and brothers, as well as her
October 5, 1990

parents, lived among the Mohawk people for four years. Her sisters and brothers went to school there with all their schoolmates being of the Caughnawaga Mohawk people. What she understood from that and as conveyed to me over the years, is that the use of their own language was essential for their identity, their self-respect and their survival for what they think they are, one of the first nations of Canada.
In that they are the same as us.

My colleague has said that in that they are the same as us. Certainly, as a person of English language origin I feel a very strong need to maintain the English language, but I do not feel it is threatened at the present time.
What has changed to some extent recently and what has impressed me this year is the very strong drive for determination of Canada's First Nations to control their own culture. Sometimes this gets into a discussion of words such as sovereignty, and people wonder if it means control of the army and so on. That is not before us today. There is nothing being proposed by the First Nations in this matter and nothing being proposed by the amendment by the hon. member for Vancouver East that in any way challenges or threatens the responsibility and authority of the existing governments of Canada. Rather, it is the opposite. What many Canadians are now beginning to learn and realize is that it was not properly presented when we went to school 30, 40 or 50 years ago in our Canadian history.
Over two centuries ago, King George III made a solemn agreement with some of the First Nations which has been applied to many of the others, that there would be a fiduciary responsibility, or an obligation to act positively on behalf of the First Nations. This would mean a legal obligation to consult the First Nations when the Government of Canada or any of its subordinate governments is initiating some change in its programs that might affect them. This was an undertaking which is still an obligation to this day of the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces. It is an obligation which has been grossly neglected or even denied far too often in past years.
Government Orders
When the government talks about the rule of law and law being applicable to everyone in Canada, with no one having the right to take the law into his own hands, it is very unfortunate to see the government doing exactly what it says no one can do, that is, simply abrogating its responsibility in this sense of consulting the First Nations before doing something that would affect the teaching of their language.
Therefore, I believe it would be a small evidence of good faith if the government would listen to the request of the First Nations on this point. These evidences are needed. We heard a speech by the Prime Minister promising to do all sorts of wonderful things for the First Nations if a small band of people at Kanesatake would simply lay down their arms. They have laid down their arms. They are now in the custody, that is those of them who were sought for custody, of the authorities recognized by this government. Now is the time for this government to show its good faith and give unanimous consent. We have heard from the official opposition, the Liberal Party. We now wish to have unanimous consent completed by the government.
In light of the Prime Minister's promises of a few days ago, I ask that the control of the teaching of the aboriginal languages be left with the aboriginal people, to be carried on in co-operation with the Canadian government on a consultative basis, and not to be handed to the bureaucrats of some institution that is now to be created so that may do what they please about aboriginal languages. The aboriginal peoples will have no recognized right in the minds of those bureaucrats to any say in what is done.
Please recognize the kind of desperation that is reflected in the words and in the actions of the First Nations at this time. They feel they are faced with extinction, as has been pointed out in the letter read by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Recognize that and do not exasperate them further. Do not exacerbate their fears further by this quite unnecessary insistence that if the government's appointed officials in this heritage language institution wish to do something or other with the aboriginal languages, they are free to do it. Please respect the rights granted two centuries ago by the King of England, then an authority of this land, and the promises so grandly made by the Prime Minister only a few days ago.

October 5, 1990
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut]

I am glad to be able to speak to the member for Vancouver East's amendment with regard to the heritage languages. The Inuktitut language must move forward and be alive for generations to come. As my colleague for Western Arctic stated, aboriginal languages are being eroded and therefore need to be encouraged. We have to ensure that future generations keep our language, and through it our culture, alive and well.

Although the Prime Minister and the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs over the last few weeks have been telling the people of Canada how much more they are going to do for the aboriginal people of this country, it just drives home the point that their promises may not mean too much when my colleague for Western Arctic is denied unanimous consent to go ahead with Bill C-269 on the issue of aboriginal languages.
It is an issue too with the government House leader as to what priorities or what recognition aboriginal languages have. It is indeed a very serious issue on the part of the aboriginal people. The issue of language, the issue of being able to move forward with our language is a fundamental part of our culture. I am sure that the House leader would be just as happy if we just went away and did not drive home the point that we do indeed have aboriginal rights.

speechtext:

The central issue for Canadians is the issue of trust. For months and months, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have been saying that there are no alternatives to the goods and services tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have said that there have been no realistic alternatives because we have studied Mr. Brooks' proposal and the single tax proposal. They do not make sense. It involves putting a much heavier tax burden on small business.
My hon. friend says that it simplifies the system. It simplifies one aspect of the system in that there is a one-page form, but it omits a number of other schedules to the preparation of the tax which help business people and individuals prepare their tax returns. They can avoid mistakes that are going to complicate the whole situation.
Is the hon. member suggesting that we should increase the tax rates for low income people? Is the hon. member saying that we should increase the rate of tax for small business? Is the hon. member saying we should put a far heavier burden on income tax and remove taxation totally from consumption?
Privilege
He says that, yes, he would like to do that. That would put a tremendous reduction to the incentive for working, for saving, and for investing in the country. These are things that are very important in the development of this economy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: A very brief reply.

Strong language.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before Question Period the hon. member for Nunatsiaq had the floor. I will recognize the hon. member.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to continue with the amendment of
the hon. member for Vancouver East to the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act.
I would like to quote from some letters that arrived in my office with regard to the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act. This one is from the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, which is the representative organization for all the Inuit in Canada. I will read part of the letter which was written to the Secretary of State of Canada. It states:
Unlike other minorities in Canada, we have no homelands in which our language and our culture can flourish, other than the Canadian North. As native people, we have special rights by virtue of our aboriginal status. These rights have been enshrined in the Canadian Constitution and are part of the laws, customs and treaties of the land. Although these aboriginal rights have not been fully defined, it is certain that they will include the right to the protection and enhancement of native languages and cultures.
That is the feeling of the Inuit Thpirisat of Canada and all the Inuit, that aboriginal languages have to be recognized by themselves and not as part of a larger group of languages.
I would also like to read another letter from the National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations to the hon. members of Parliament, which in part says:
Although we understand Aboriginal languages are not excluded from the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act, First Nations do not wish to be included in the definition of "Heritage Languages" in Bill C-37. We are the "founding" languages of Canada, and given the precarious future of our endangered languages, require a separate Aboriginal Languages Foundation/Institute.
It is with these kinds of letters and the support that we have from the various aboriginal groups that we press forward not to be included in the Canadian Heritage Languages Act but that aboriginal languages be recognized on their own merits as the founding languages of this nation.
Earlier this year the Government of Canada slashed its funding to the aboriginal communications sector. When that occurred several things happened which cut back on either the education of aboriginal languages through the media or in other ways caused us suffering.
I would again like to refer to a copy of the press release by the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation which is the TV arm of the Inuit Communications Society. It says in the press release issued on February 22, 1990:
The Inuil Broadcasting Corporation (IBC) may lose more than a quarter of its funding as a result of the new federal budget. The $600,000.00 cut will have an immediate and devastating impact on Canada's leading aboriginal television network.
October 5, 1990

That speaks for itself. The Government of Canada, through the government House leader, in refusing to recognize Bill C-269, an act to recognize aboriginal languages within the Constitution, is really telling us what priorities it has in terms of aboriginal issues. It tells the aboriginal people that it has put forward the aboriginal issues of the day to recognize the aboriginal peoples' concerns, but it does not want to follow through by recognizing the need for aboriginal languages to be recognized in the Constitution by themselves.
Again, I would also like to quote from a friend of mine, Blandina Makkik, from the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation who calls the $600,000 cut to the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation spiritual genocide, which is very descriptive of how the people feel.
I would like to tell the Canadian people how important it is that the aboriginal languages be recognized because, as everyone knows, language is part of your culture.
I am sure that the government House leader never had to cope with the problem of not being able to speak his own language because he was forbidden to do so, as we were when we were in residential schools or when we were in public schools. I am sure that he never had to struggle with that. I am sure that he would never understand why we feel we have to be recognized separately and on our own. Again I would like to quote an article from the National Aboriginal Communications Society on the issue of cutting back on communications, which reads:
It is particularly important that Native people have access to communications giving the Aboriginal perspective during a time when such issues as self-government, Aboriginal title and equality rights are being debated.
Madam Speaker, those are the few issues that we have and I thank you for your indulgence.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate. First, along with the number of speakers who have spoken concerning the importance of the aboriginal languages I want to be on record as stating how important I believe that this is.
Government Orders
Having an opportunity to travel in the Northwest Territories and Yukon during the Charest commission on the Meech Lake Accord-McKenna proposals, it was a great experience for me to sit in the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories where some 27 languages were being translated during the debate. The issue of aboriginal languages is one that is extremely important, but unfortunately this is not the issue we are debating today, although some who may be watching this debate may think that is exactly what we are debating.
What we are debating is an amendment to clause 2 of Bill C-37. I would just like to read from clause 2:
"heritage language" means a language, other than one of the
official languages of Canada, that contributes to the linguistic
heritage of Canada,-
That is how clause 2 in part reads and the amendment wishes to indicate that this does not include an aboriginal language of Canada.
I would just like to go back to the history of this clause. We had a lot of discussion in the committee on Bill C-37 about this very aspect of this clause. I am a bit surprised that we are debating it again at report stage, because we had such an extensive debate at committee stage concerning whether or not aboriginal languages should be included as part of the Heritage Languages Institute. When we reflect on the previously proposed legislation, Bill C-152 which was brought before the House of Commons prior to the election of 1988, this bill, practically in its entirety, was brought in, during the last Parliament, and was not passed because of the election.
In that previous proposed legislation aboriginal languages were not included. It was not stated whether they were included or not included; it was not mentioned. Then when we got to committee on Bill C-152, the Liberal Party and the NDP were insisting that aboriginal languages should be included. In fact they made a number of motions and at report stage a Liberal member amended the bill to say that the retention and use of languages including native and aboriginal languages should be included in this bill.
So here we are: we introduced this Bill C-37 into this Parliament. We have gone through committee stage. We have had extensive discussion about it. Now the Liberals and the NDP have completely reversed themselves from what their position was just a short time ago. I am

October 5, 1990
Government Orders
actually quite surprised that they would make such a big change in their position in such a short time.
I want to state briefly the purpose of this institute. What is this institute supposed to do for heritage languages? Well, it is supposed to promote and develop the field of heritage language learning in Canada. It is to undertake public education, and develop and disseminate Canadian oriented learning materials, assist in the development of programs to improve standards of heritage language instruction, and carry out research activities of importance to heritage language learning in general.
The institute will be established in Edmonton and will work closely with organizations, individuals, and groups from across the country, consulting with community-based organizations, educational institutions, and the provincial and territorial governments to ensure that all those who are concerned with heritage language training benefit from the activities of the institute.
This will be a charitable foundation as well as being supported by the Government of Canada. It will receive financial support from the private sector. We hope that everyone involved will be very much into making this institute the tremendous place that we think it is going to be in order to have the heritage languages expanded.
I understand what the member for Western Arctic is saying concerning Bill C-269. I wish we were debating Bill C-269 right now, but we are not. However, I think it would be very valuable to have the merits of Bill C-269 debated but unfortunately that is not what is before us today. What is before us is whether we are actually going to bar somebody from being part of the heritage language institute.
The bill states that heritage language will mean language other than the official languages that contribute to the linguistic heritage of Canada. Therefore, we do not want to exclude anybody. It does not necessarily include everybody. We have not named all the languages, but it is open-ended. If groups want to come to get research material, there will be an opportunity to do it.
Madam Speaker, I believe that the way the bill as amended in committee now stands before the House is the appropriate definition of heritage language.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I feel privileged to participate in today's debate on an act to establish a Canadian Heritage Languages Institute and particularly to follow the very thoughtful amendment of my hon. colleague from Vancouver East which suggests that we amend the bill by saying "Canada and does not include aboriginal languages of Canada".
I really want to associate myself with the comments made by my hon. colleague from Vancouver East as well as my colleagues from Comox-Albemi and Spadina on this issue because it seems to be totally inappropriate that we would not include those languages of our first citizens in with heritage languages generally.
To make my point, I want to quote from Mr. Phil Fontaine, the provincial leader of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs, who on July 14 of this year said the following: "We, the original people of this country have inherited through the oral traditions of our forefathers 55 distinct original languages. Fifty-two of these original languages of Canada are now on the brink of extinction. Unlike you," meaning the non-aboriginal peoples of the country, "we cannot retrieve these languages from our mother country. Our mother country is Canada. What we lose in Canada we lose forever."
I think that we really have to reflect seriously on what appeared at least in the beginning to be the government's motivation to include with Italian, Norwegian, Danish and German, 53 aboriginal languages to be considered heritage languages.
Regardless of what we might do to our national heritage in terms of language, myself being Norwegian, we can always go back home and learn the language, or be introduced again to it.
We cannot do that with aboriginal languages. This is their home. This is the only place in the world where they exist. I feel particularly strongly about representation. A group of us, members of Parliament from the interior of British Columbia, met recently in the great city of Vernon. At that meeting we were privileged to welcome four of the native chiefs of our region. They explained their concern about their language. This is the Shuswap language, Madam Speaker, a name that you are
October 5, 1990

very familiar with yourself. It is one of the many languages we find in British Columbia.
I am pleased to say when I look at the list that there are 2,000 individuals who are presently speaking the Shuswap language. As the provincial leader of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs indicated, it is not one of the languages that unless something is done will not be preserved beyond the next decade or so. As a matter of fact, as I said earlier, only three of the 55 languages will remain in place unless some action is taken.
What action are we requiring? We certainly are going far beyond the suggestion of an institute. I suspect that we are getting very close to the point raised by my hon. colleague for Western Arctic in Bill C-269-which, of course, we support-calling for an aboriginal languages foundation.
The assumption we all make is that this is going to require some investment so that native people across our great country will have an opportunity to develop the necessary learning materials, provide the necessary learning infrastructure, so that young and old alike will be able to learn and become fluent in their native language. I think this is in the spirit of our country and something that we certainly ought to do as expeditiously as possible for Canada's first citizens.
I know in Kamloops the Shuswap Tribal Council has made tremendous gains in developing curriculum for kindergarten and grades beyond, in terms of the language classes as well as a cultural introduction to the reality of the native experience in central British Columbia.
The initiative the government is taking regarding Bill C-37 is one that we support obviously because of its encouragement and development of Canada's heritage languages. But again, as this amendment makes very clear, we certainly do not want to exclude the aboriginal languages of Canada from that consideration. We want to set aside a major initiative to ensure that language becomes our preoccupation in terms of assisting aboriginal people across the country. We want them to develop the necessary infrastructure to develop their own languages which will enable them to build their cultures with strength and on a good foundation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this particular section of the act, clause 6, relates to the board of directors which will actually be there to direct the activities of the Heritage Languages Institute. There will be 21 directors that will be selected from across the country.
Let us reflect for a moment on what is in the bill. How will these people be selected? They will be selected after and in such consultation with provincial governments, institutions, organizations and individuals. All those people will be consulted. It is important to read that with clause 6.(2) of the bill which says:
(2) Persons appointed to the Board must have knowledge or experience that will assist the Institute in fulfilling its purpose.
I think the amendment is looking for persons to be representing organizations and language schools. Because of the vast numbers of organizations and schools that we have, we could not have all these organizations represented because we have 21 directors.
What we need is to have an opportunity for the minister, after consultation, to appoint those persons with experience and knowledge. Geographic representation, as the member has suggested, would be taken into consideration, as well, in order to have people with a broad spectrum of skills and expertise to make this
institute the tremendous organization that we believe it will be.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in favour of the amendment in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East. We have no other choice but to support it. How can we guarantee fairness and, above all, professionalism and impartiality, in an institute where the members of the Board of directors are to be appointed on the recommendation of the minister?
Does this government intend to do what it did in the Senate and appoint its friends, who will have to respond to the priorities determined by the minister?
Madam Speaker, the institute should be able to make its own appointments, after consultation, of course, with cultural communities and teachers. I say this because they are in a position to select the people they believe are most competent and capable of performing their duties, and do not need the government's official or informal approval. I therefore support this amendment.

We have already seen evidence of great government partiality in the nominations of the members to a recent multicultural commission. Some of the members on this particular cultural commission are in absolutely no way linked or connected to any large national cultural bodies. Some, I believe, are really hacks.
Hacks? Shame!

I would even go so far as to say they represent only themselves, or perhaps the minister. They have never been involved in some instances in any way, shape, or form with any cultural community.
The bottom line on this whole institute makes one wonder if it is not a political candy to Edmonton. That is why we, as Liberals, on this side of the House are supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver East.

ency assistants are also working on the problems of Scarborough Centre.

I met people in Sarnia. I met people in Windsor. Madam Speaker, in addressing the amendment now being debated, I want to speak very briefly on it and say only two things. I want to note the great participation of members from the great city of Scarborough here today.
The mechanism that has been proposed by this amendment is a commendable one and one that conceptually has been addressed by no less than the Prime Minister himself in considering the issue of prospective appointments to the Senate. The mechanism was referred to in the Meech Lake Accord and it involves nominations or appointments by the government from a list supplied by, if I can use the term, the client group.
I cannot think of a better mechanism which would both purge any appearance of patronage that might be there in any particular appointment and at the same time serve to democratize further or bring the level of appointment making back toward the street, back to the people, the client group, who have need of the organization. For those two reasons I am in support of this amendment.
Madam Speaker, I also support the amendment by my colleague from Vancouver Centre and I think it is-
Vancouver East.

Vancouver East, sorry. I thought Vancouver Centre would be wise enough to suoport it but I may be wrong.

October 5, 1990

The reason I support it is that the method of appointment suggested in the bill is kind of the Tory top-down system of governing in Canada that I think has led a lot of people to be cynical about how government handles itself in this day and age. I think a lot of people are cynical and a lot of people are disillusioned about how government handles itself.
These kind of appointments come from the top down. They tend to be political appointments. They tend to be people who do not represent the grass roots. They tend to be people who in many cases are not even familiar with the organizations that they are supposed to be serving or with the issues they are supposed to be serving.
I recall a recent issue of The Ottawa Citizen that reported that in a single day the Government of Canada made a 108 patronage appointments. The article went through the resumes of some of those people and found out that, while some of them had a remote connection or were reappointed to an organization that they had served on before, a substantial number of those people were simply political hacks and flacks and not the best people available to serve the interests of Canadian citizens or, in this case, the ethnic groups or the linguistic groups who need to be served by this heritage language legislation.
It is long overdue that we change in law the way that we appoint these people. The way we should appoint these people is to make them responsible to the groups from which they come and that they be nominated or selected from the groups from which they come and the groups which they serve. This bottom-up approach is the approach we should be looking at if we are trying to restore credibility in government. If we are trying to restore confidence in government and in institutions such as the one we are setting up here, the Eleritage Languages Institute, then we should really be setting up a structure and a process in this legislation which allows nomination of the people who are going to be serving on this board from the representative groups, from the groups that they are going to be serving, rather than having the campaign managers from the last Tory campaign or the wives or husbands of former Tory members of Parliament, as we saw in that article in The Ottawa Citizen a few weeks ago. Let us have people who really
know the field that they are working in. Let us have people who really understand and know the constituency that they are serving.
I think that the suggestion by my colleague from Vancouver East is the kind of process that is going to result in that happening. What we will have if we adopt this amendment and adopt this process is an institute that we can all be proud of and that the people who will be served by this institute can also be proud of, have confidence in, and appear themselves to be stakeholders in.
