speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-54, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (joinder of counts) be read the third time and passed.
She said: Madam Speaker, I want to thank all parties who made a contribution to the consideration and drafting of this bill at all stages. More specifically, I would like to thank my former opposition critics, and I
October 5, 1990

hope to have the same satisfactory relationship with the new critics.

This bill comes as a result of the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Regina v. Vaillancourt. I hope that, through these amendments, justice will be expedited and, that the modernization of this law will bring it into line with today's requirements.

Madam Speaker, it was a very brief and succinct address by the Minister of Justice.
The bill we are debating here is itself a rather brief and succinct bill. One might say it was a simple housekeeping bill in relation to the Criminal Code, but I am afraid that it is never possible to call amendments to the Criminal Code simple housekeeping. In that act, we address issues and procedures that belly up right against our rights and freedoms as citizens, and our conduct among each other in a civilized, ordered society.
I feel that it is necessary to address each of the amendments as proposed albeit that they are short and brief.
The first amendment proposed by the government deals with the deletion from the code of subsection 230(d). That subsection is one of four constructive murder charges currently in the Criminal Code.
After due consideration, the Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that that section varies or conflicts with our Charter of Rights and therefore has been struck by the courts from the code. Today the government is asking and has asked in this bill that the section be formally deleted from the code.
The only issue that arises in relation to this action by the government is whether or not the government should have addressed removing or deleting subsections (a), (b) and (c) of the same section, because those subsections deal with the same issue of constructive murder from different perspectives.
Having read judicial comment of the last few years, I think it is fair to say that constructive murder, no matter what perspective it comes from, is going to be a difficult debt with the rights and freedoms set out in our charter.
There are existing before the high courts in Canada appeals dealing with various of these constructive mur-
Govemment Orders
der subsections, and the court will make a ruling. The real issue here-I have simply raised the flag-is whether or not the government might have shown a bit more leadership in addressing head on those rights and freedoms, those charter issues related to subsections (a), (b) and (c), dealt with them now, got them out of the way and saved the courts a whole lot of time.
The flip side of that coin is that we as legislators may well benefit from the judicial interpretations that we will be offered from the courts over the next few months. That may help the Minister of Justice, the Department of Justice and members in the House to reach better and more informed conclusions on those subsections.
Moving on to the second part of the bill, an old rule that had been imposed ages ago prohibited the joinder of a murder count with a count alleging another indictable offence. In the old days, I guess that was quite a fair rule because in the old days a conviction for murder, nine times out of 10, resulted in some pretty dire consequences. The world has changed, we have changed and while in many cases the consequences for the convicted may not be so dire, in terms of capital punishment, there is a sense that we are more capable of dealing with the sophisticated legal issues that lie behind the law as it relates to murder and the procedures related to prosecutions for murder.
So that old rule which says you cannot join any count with a murder count will now be changed to the following: in practical terms, where the murder count arises out of a fact situation where another offence may have been committed, the Crown may join the murder count with a count alleging another offence. Second, where the accused, himself or herself, consents to having the murder count tried with other counts, whether or not they arise out of the same fact situation, the joinder may take place.
The first real reason that brought us all to address joinder, notwithstanding the old rule, was the appearance of cases of failures to complete prosecutions, failure to complete the delivery of justice, as a result of the non-joinder rule. As a result, there was a feeling that the courts, the system, the taxpayer and the accused could all be better off if the courts were permitted to try murder and other counts together. All of the witnesses would be brought in and the facts set out, thereby precluding the need for subsequent trials or breaking

Government Orders
trials up into sections with witnesses having to attend much more frequently.
The efficacy reason prompted the review of the rule, the Law Reform Commission did some excellent work reviewing it, the issue has been canvassed by academics, the courts and lawyers, and the net result is that there seems to be, on balance, a feeling that the old joinder rule should be abandoned.
The major alleged problem with abandoning the nonjoinder rule is that accused may be prejudiced by this. Of course, that was an argument in why the non-joinder rule was there in the first place, but we must point out that in every single case where a murder indictment is prosecuted, an accused has the right to ask for severance of the counts. There is not likely a judge in this country who is not aware of the significance of possible prejudice to an accused in a murder trial and there is not likely a Crown prosecutor in the country who is not aware of that. At the commencement of each murder trial, there is that opportunity for the accused and his or her counsel to raise that with the trial judge and, if the trial judge believes that prejudice may occur, severance can be ordered and the trial for murder may proceed on its own, without the joinder with other counts.
We in the opposition, having stated that we have looked at these concerns, feel that on balance we can support this bill brought forward by the government.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill, which has been handed to me just recently, and to deliver my first speech as new justice critic for the New Democratic Party. The bill is now at third reading. I want to, first of all, say to my friend opposite, the Minister of Justice, who comes from a riding near where I live, that I will try to be as constructive as possible in dealing with justice matters. I know that we are dealing with some very important issues here for people in Canada. We both respect that. I may disagree with the minister, but I respect her a great deal. That is the nicest thing I am about to say about her ever. Now I will get on with the bill.
As I understand, Bill C-54 was tabled on December 14, 1989. It was approved in principle by the House at second reading. It went to committee. I have had a chance to look at some of the committee hearings. It is
now back to the House for report stage and third reading. I believe we are now on third reading.
The bill would amend the Criminal Code of Canada, the Criminal Code of course being the book that has all the criminal laws in Canada. It applies throughout the country, criminal law being a federal matter.
The government, of course, has to update the Criminal Code regularly, and now even more so in response to judgments of the courts which under the Charter of Rights can declare sections of the Criminal Code unconstitutional. Part of that aspect is involved in the government response in this bill.
Clause 1 of Bill C-54, as I understand it, would repeal one of the prescribed elements for constructive murder under section 230 of the Criminal Code of Canada. Clause 2 would revise section 589 of the Criminal Code in favour of a less restrictive regime for the joinder of counts where murder is charged.
I want to briefly deal with both of those changes. First, constructive murder. Section 230 of the Criminal Code, as I said, sets forth the offence known as constructive murder. It has been defined as a death that occurs in connection with the commission of a criminal offence. It is construed as having been intentional even though, on the facts, the accused did not mean the cause of death. Let me try and explain that in lay person's terms, if I might.
To be guilty of murder, you have to cause death. You have to intend to cause death. It is a very simple principle in criminal law that you have to do the act. In Latin that is called the actus reus. You also need to have to intention to do the act. That is called mens rea, your mind. You have to put your mind to it. It is quite simple. You have to do the act, and you have to intend to do the act.
Let us take a situation, God forbid, where my colleague and I decided to commit a robbery. We sit and plan the act of the robbery. We do the act of the robbery, and we intend to do the act of the robbery. During the act of the robbery, I have a gun. It is an armed robbery. Someone interferes or intervenes, or something happens, and I shoot someone in the course of the robbery, like someone in the bank, for example. That person is

killed. I, on those facts, would be guilty of murder. I intended to do the act. I did the act of murder.
My friend was there for the robbery, but he did not intend to do the murder. Under this section of the code he in fact could be guilty of murder as well because he is constructively said to intend it. By the mere fact of participating in the armed robbery, he is thought of as having maybe thought that there could have been a possibility that the gun would be used and someone would be killed.
I was a criminal lawyer at one point in my checkered career. We always felt very uncomfortable with this section because people could be convicted of murder even though they did not intend to do murder. That is against the basic principles of criminal law.
I will give another example which the Library of Parliament has given us in a little different way. It said, for example, that it would be described as constructive murder within the meaning of section 230 if a perpetrator, while fleeing the scene of robbery, dropped his weapon, which accidentally went off and in the process killed an innocent bystander. It is another example of where one did not really intend to kill the person but it happened in the course of a criminal act. That was a lay person's description of how this section works.
The Supreme Court, in the case of Vaillancourt v. the Queen, in fact threw out this section, and I think quite properly.
It seems to me there is a problem with the bill. The question arises: Are there other sections of this particular section of the Criminal Code that the court might also throw out? I believe-and the minister can correct me if I am wrong-that the bill only deals with section 230(d). That is only one section that deals with constructive murder.
I believe there are other cases before the courts, and again the minister can correct me if I am wrong. What happens if the other cases are thrown out? Will we have the same problem with the other sections of the bill?
Government Orders
Will we have to come back to Parliament to deal with it? Perhaps we should deal with it all now.
The Law Reform Commission of Canada in its 1984 publication entitled Homicide, (Working Paper 33) stated that it found the whole section 230 is objectionable and should be abolished, and I quote:
To treat an unintentional killer as though he intended to kill involves the criminal law in artificiality and fictions and in the injustice of not treating significantly different cases differently.
We think that constructive murder should be abolished, that the rules contained in paragraph 212(c) and section 213 (now paragraph 229(d) and section 230) should have no place within our criminal law, and that killings where death is neither intended nor foreseen should be excluded from the category of "intentional" homicide whether or not they are brought about in furtherance of some other offence.
They made the following recommendation:
"Intentional" homicide should apply only to killings done with actual intent to kill, and cases of constructive intent should be excluded from this category.
My point is that this bill does not exclude all the possible cases of unintended murder. My position is, along with the Law Reform Commission report, that intentional homicide should only apply to killings done with actual intent to kill, and cases where we have constructive intent should be taken out of our law. I think it is bad law and always was bad law. That is my first point and that is one of the reasons why we will not be supporting the bill. However, I understand that the bill could pass today on division.
Soon.

The member says: "Soon", but I want to explain to the member-and I am trying to do it in very simple language-what is involved in a very complicated
bin.
The House will recall that when I started my speech I said that there were two points to the bill. Let us deal with the second point. The second point is that the bill would revise section 589 of the Criminal Code in favour of a less restrictive regime for joinder of counts where murder is charged.
Here is the problem, and maybe I can make it simple-there can be a prejudice to the accused if one joins a murder count with a lot of other counts because murder is so bad and looks so bad to a jury that the jury can be prejudiced. This is what disturbs me about this section.
I have a legal opinion from the firm of Rosen and Fleming, barristers in Toronto, that was obtained by my

Government Orders
predecessor, the hon. member for Burnaby with respect to this bill. I just want to read what these learned lawyers have said. I will just read this section:
If the proposed legislation is passed, the above general principles relating to the joinder of counts generally will apply. A person accused of murder will have the same onus to demonstrate a manifest need for severance. However, since the proposed legislation requires that in such cases the other offences to be added to the indictment must rise out of the same transaction, and because it follows that evidence concerning one offence will probably be admissible on the others because they are so related, it will be virtually impossible for an accused to meet the onus. If convicted, the rights of the accused on appeal will be subject to the limitations noted above of appellate review of the exercise of judicial discretion. The protection of severance cited by the proponents of the amendment is illusory at best.
It continues:
Proponents of the amendment suggest that the accused will suffer no prejudice by joinder of counts since, if convicted of murder and any other related offences, the convictions for these other offences may be stayed pursuant to the decisions of Kienapple v. R. and R. v. Prince or the sentences imposed for them will be concurrent to the mandatory life sentence which follows the murder conviction. This position totally ignores the potential for prejudice at trial which comes from the overloading of an indictment.
Here are four examples of how the prejudice arises, but let me just go back a step. If someone gets charged with some offences, there is an indictment preferred by the Crown, Her Majesty, an indictment. It is take to court and the person has to answer to the indictment and is read the indictment.
I was in court in Vancouver just recently in the Inderjit Singh Reyat trial, the trial of the citizen who is accused of making the bomb that went on the CP flight to Tokyo which blew up and killed two baggage handlers in Tokyo; a real tragic case. The trial is being held right now in Vancouver, as I speak. Mr. Reyat was arraigned before the court and an indictment was read. There were a number of counts on that indictment: you are charged with this, you are charged with that, you are charged with this, how do you plead. What we are talking about in this clause of the bill is how that indictment works.
What could happen is that someone appears before the court and is charged with a number of offences. The defence counsel on behalf of the accused could stand up and say: I move that we sever one of the counts off, that we have another trial at another place or at another time
on this particular count, and that we proceed in this trial with these counts. The reason a severance is allowed-it is at the discretion of the trial judge usually-is that it is allowed because it may prejudice the accused or prejudice a fair trial.
I think we have the best system known, so far invented in the world, for criminal justice. It is not perfect, but it is an ancient and honourable tradition in the British system that has been developed. That is why these matters are so important, and this deals with severance.
Here is the legal opinion that I was citing. Here is what they say were the problems with this section. I put it forward for the consideration of the Minister of Justice. It reads:
(a)	The jury will be distracted by the numerous other counts included in the indictment and will fail to appreciate the importance of what is at stake in the murder charge.
This is putting a murder charge with a whole bunch of other charges: robbery, assault, whatever. The first point is that the accused to be prejudiced because the jury will look at all these other counts and it will not totally focus on the one count, the one murder count, and these other counts could prejudice the trial on the murder count. In referring to many counts, it continues:
(b)	An accused who faces a multiple count indictment which begins with the offence of murder will be viewed by the jury, even before the evidence is called, as a person of disreputable character.
In other words, if you are charged with murder that is pretty serious. The jury looks at you being charged with murder as you come before the jury. However, if you are charged with murder and assault and robbery and having a weapon and so on, the jury may be prejudiced and say that is a pretty bad person; they have been charged with all those counts, all those other things; maybe they are the kind of person who might murder. That is a prejudice. That is why there is a danger in allowing all these multiple counts. That is why there is a danger in this amendment to the code. That is why we are opposing this. It continues:
(c)	The rule concerning the admissibility of similar fact evidence will be circumvented by the prosecution, since evidence admissible on one count, but not necessarily admissible on another will nevertheless be admitted before the jury. As noted above, the relevance of the evidence to the one count and the fact that all the counts are related will be cited as the reason to deny severance which might otherwise relieve the prejudice.

Again there is talk of similar evidence. Evidence on one count tends to become evidence on the other count and we get into problems with similar fact evidence. Not only on the surface could it be prejudice to a jury, but some of the evidence that comes into one count will filter into another count and there will be further possibility of prejudice. It continues:
(d)	The evidence of other related criminal conduct which may be admissible as part of the narrative relating to the homicide,-
That is the story leading to the murder case. It goes on:
-will now be used to convict the accused of specific offences-
That is, the robbery, the possession of the gun, the breaking and entering, and so on. It continues:
- rather than permitting the jury to consider the evidence and its weight, if any, on the issue of liability for murder only.
The real issue is that murder is such a serious charge it should be tried alone. Alternatively, if it is tried with the other offences, such great prejudice can result both in naming the different counts so the jury sees all the other charges or by the similar fact evidence coming in as the Crown attorney tries to prove those different counts. That is about the simplest way I can put it. For those two reasons there could be some real problems.
I had a chance this week to meet some criminal lawyers. Among them was Clay Ruby, one of the top criminal lawyers in Canada, and some other criminal lawyers in Toronto as well. They expressed to me their concern about this particular section on the joinder of counts.
For those two reasons we in the New Democratic Party are opposed to Bill C-54.1 think I have set out, as best I can, the reasons for that opposition in some detail. I have tried to translate it a little bit away from the language of the law to the language of ordinary people.
I do not know if the government will hear any more speakers. I do remind the government that I did raise the point that we might, even if this is passed, have to revisit the section if the courts declare other aspects of section
Government Orders
230 of the Criminal Code of Canada unconstitutional as they did with section 230 subsection (d).

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to respond briefly to some of the comments made by my colleague for Port Moody-Coquitlam.
I certainly take his point that this is a very interesting area of the law in recent jurisprudence. Martineau, Vaillancourt, and other cases have certainly changed the practice and have been instructive to governments. Since the committee studied this bill, the provisions of section (a) which are being removed from section 230 of the code have been struck down.
My colleague raises a number of interesting questions. I want to say at the beginning, though, that the whole law with respect to homicide is under intensive review in the Department of Justice now. Some of the comments that he raises will be addressed in a more comprehensive framework.
What we are dealing with here is an effort to try to address a very specific problem, which is the need to amend the Criminal Code to remove the culpable murder provisions, as they have since been struck down by the courts. Paragraphs (b) and (c) which remain are possibly at risk we well. I would be the first to concede that.
This area of the law is a very challenging one because it requires us to balance a number of interests. When we look at the whole idea of joining counts, we look at the question of what will be brought before a court.
When my hon. colleague says that murder should always be tried on its own, that may or may not be the case. The point is that if murder is the wrong count to be brought, then any other count would have to be brought separately. Are we going to look at the administration of justice as a kind of all-or-nothing situation and try to determine the appropriate count, if Crown counsel is of the view that there is in fact sufficient evidence to convict on a murder count if the jury does not agree with them, or the judge does not agree with them? Does that mean that is the end of the story for making someone responsible for events rising out of a particular transaction?

Government Orders
We have a jurisprudential framework within which the law is applied. We make reference to the principle of what I learned in law school to call Kienapple. It derives from a decision of the Supreme Court to protect people from a multiplicity of counts on a particular event.
So there is a jurisprudential framework which I think does protect. There is no question that there are challenges to a trial court judge in instructing the jury or instructing himself or herself if the case is heard before a judge in sorting out the evidence and I would not underestimate those.
However, I do not think those arguments are sufficient to justify defeating the bill. They simply point out that there are a number of interests to be balanced, the interest not just in the efficiency of the administration of justice in avoiding a multiplicity of trial processes and all that that involved in terms of recalling witnesses and trying to keep a case intact, but also in subjecting an accused to a multiplicity of processes which I think can be very difficult and-I was going to say in trying-but it very difficult and stressful. What we are attempting to do with this is simply address what is a very explicit issue.
I want to close by repeating that the whole law with respect to homicide is under review and I am looking forward to participation. The remarks made by my colleague in the Liberal Party were also very much to the point. He is not the official critic in this area so he will not be offended, I hope, when I say that I look forward to the participation of all interested members of this House, particularly the critics, and particularly my colleague the critic from the New Democratic Party who is a criminal lawyer of some considerable experience.
I have always found the expression criminal lawyer an awkward one to use. One tends to say the words very quickly and run them together so that there is no misunderstanding of what is involved. While he may have exhausted his store of nice things to say about me, I suspect that every once in a while he will have something nice to say about my dad with whom he worked in that particular line of work and with whom he has a relationship of very mutual respect.
The hon. member came into the House after I had made my introductory comments. Had he not done so he would have heard my expressed wish to work very closely with my new critics. I think that I am very lucky to have a
colleague of his distinction at the bar to be the critic and to be participating in our attempts to make the criminal law both fair and consistent with modem developments in modem society. I hope that he will continue to be involved in that process.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the minister for her remarks.
There is a story of two criminal lawyers who go on a cruise. They are arguing during a beautiful midnight dinner and get so into the argument, as criminal lawyers always do, that they fall overboard. People were exclaiming, "Oh, my God. This is terrible. This in shark-infested waters." Suddenly the sharks come up and form a line for them and they swim right back. One of the people on the ship says: "It is a miracle". The wife of one of the criminal lawyers said, "No, no. It is just professional courtesy".
The only point I want to make to the minister is this. She says section B and section C are at risk by the court. If the court holds them inoperative too, as they have done with section D, and I think there is a real possibility of this, then I say to the government why proceed now, why not wait until those cases are dealt with. It seems to me a little odd that we would deal with this so quickly.

Madam Speaker, I rise for only 30 seconds.
Listening to lawyers talk about legal points is beyond some of us. I must admit that I do not know what joinder's accounts are. I do know that my constituents and many of our constituents are concerned about the increasing use of guns in violent crime.
What sounded earlier like a discussion about the reduction of available sentences and penalties becomes clearer when the minister answers the question that this
October 5, 1990

is a matter ordered by the courts. Therefore, I have no problem with what is before us.
I simply want to put on the record the sense of a lot of our constituents as the homicide review goes through, that we do not need weaker penalties for those who accidentally or otherwise involve firearms in killing folks. We need stronger ones.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rod Laporte (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-230, an act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act (oats and barley), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise today to speak to this bill.
The Canadian Wheat Board is an institution that has been part of the western Canadian agricultural way of life for over half a century. It is one of those institutions that receives the support of not only farmers but of a tremendous majority of western Canadians from all walks of life.
It is looked at longingly by producers from outside the board's jurisdiction. These include not only Canadian farmers in areas outside western Canada, but many Americans speak highly of the efficiency of the Canadian Wheat Board. In short, it is an institution that is held in high regard by a majority of people who know of its function.
The Canadian Wheat Board was created in 1935 with jurisdiction over the sale of wheat. This power was extended in 1943 when the government closed the wheat futures market, thus making the Wheat Board the sole marketer of wheat in western Canada.
The power of the Canadian Wheat Board was expanded in 1949 to include barley and oats. Unfortunately, the reason that we are here today is that barley and oats were not given the same protection under the act that wheat was. In order to remove wheat, the matter must be debated in the House. Only Parliament can change the board's jurisdiction regarding wheat. With barley and oats the Cabinet can, of its own discretion, without any consultation with the House or with anybody else, alter or remove the board's power with the right to market these two commodities. This is exactly what the Cabinet did through the recommendation of the Minister of

October 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
State for Grains and Oilseeds in February 1989 when the removal of oats from the board's jurisdiction was announced.
I believe and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party believe that the Canadian Wheat Board is an excellent example of a social democratic program. It provides producers with a marketing system that works to the benefit of all farmers. As individuals functioning in the open market, producers are competing with giants such as Continental and with Cargill.
Agricultural markets are volatile because of the unpredictable production fluctuations, because of the large number of independent producers and because of the large number of consumers. Those people who have knowledge of the market situation are at a definite advantage. Information about agricultural markets is costly and not equally available. Companies such as Cargill and others pay a lot of money for this information and they keep that information close to their chest and use it to their own advantage. Therefore they have a definite and a distinct advantage over the thousands of individual farmers who have to rely largely on the public media for their information.
The Canadian Wheat Board neutralizes this inequity and is able to deal with the Cargills of this world on an equal footing. The only time that the government has to in fact incur a loss is when a deficit pool is run, because the Canadian Wheat Board is paid for by farmers and it functions for the benefit of farmers.
When I say the only time that the government is involved with any payment is with respect to a deficit pool, I mean for those Canadians who are watching or those members who may not be aware. Every year the Canadian Wheat Board sets an initial prices that it will pay for a particular grain, be it wheat or barley and previously oats. This is the price that the farmer is guaranteed to receive for his grain regardless of what time of year he delivers his grain and regardless of the world price at that particular time. If at the end of the year the board has sold all the producer's grain for a higher rate than the initial price it paid to the farmer originally, then a final payment is made. Thus, all farmers receive the same price for their particular grain whether it is delivered in January, or June, or September, or any other time of the year.
If on occasion a particular grain is sold below the initial price, then there is a deficit and that is when the government makes up that difference. This has only happened on rare occasions. It should be noted as well that with respect to the initial price; it is the government that sets the initial price; it is not the Wheat Board. It is controlled by the government. It is announced by the government and it controls what the initial price will be. Other than that, the Wheat Board is self-perpetuating financially and it is paid for by the some 140,000 permit book holders throughout western Canada.
Why did the government choose to remove oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board? It certainly was not for budgetary reasons. As I indicated the Wheat Board is self-financing. When I and other members in this House asked the government why it had taken this step, it was indicated to me on several occasions, and in fact the Minister of Agriculture indicated to me last year with a straight face I might add, that he had had extensive consultations over a long period of time and that it was what the fanning industry wanted. They wanted oats to be removed. They said they were niche markets. They claimed that the Wheat Board could not meet those niche markets properly.
I cannot say the minister lied because that is unparliamentary but let me say that he carefully chose his facts and he considered which facts to pay attention to and which facts to ignore. Whom did he consult? In answer to a question I asked in the House on May 4, 1989, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking for the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, indicated that the government had consulted the United Grain Growers Limited and the Western Canadian Wheat Growers' Association. That is fair because oat producers are included in those. But he went on to mention the Western Barley Growers' Association, the Prairie Canola Growers' Association, the Alberta Pork Producers Development Corporation, and the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission. He consulted with the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission to see whether oats should be removed from the Canadian Wheat Board, and it said yes. It consulted with the Prairie Cattlemen's Association, the Manitoba Farm Business Association, the Manitoba Hog Producers Marketing Board, and the Saskatchewan Pork Marketing Board.
October 5, 1990

That is all very well, but what the minister did not say and, in fact, what the government has never said or acknowledged is that there are a number of other groups that it did not consult with. In fact, at no time or no where did the government indicate-perhaps it did, but it did not indicate-that it consulted with some of the largest grain organizations in Canada, namely the pools, the Alberta Wheat Pool, the Manitoba Wheat Pool and the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. It also did not consult with the National Farmers Union. The National Farmers Union is opposed to the move, as are the Prairie wheat pools.
It does not mention the fact that it did not consult with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which is one of the largest agricultural groups. It is an umbrella group of many organizations for the country. If it had consulted with the CFA, it would have been told that the CFA had passed a resolution calling for the government not to remove oats from the Canadian Wheat Board without the producers first voting on that issue.
What do farmers think of the claim that the government indicated it had consulted with farmers? That can be answered by a Decima poll that was conducted shortly after the announcement made by the government. In fact, Decima did a report, and I am quoting from that report at page 10 where it states: "fully 76 per cent of respondents believed that the government undertook inadequate consultation with farmers before it made its decision to remove oats from the marketing activities of the Canadian Wheat Board". It goes on to state: "substantial majorities in each of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta concur that the government failed to consult with farmers on this issue in any significant manner."
So, farmers feel they were not consulted. The people who grow oats feel they were not consulted. The Wheat Board's 140,000 permit book holders felt they were not consulted by a large majority, 76 per cent.
The report goes on to indicate what farmers would have told the government had they been consulted. At page 10 the report states: "A substantial majority, 63 per cent, of western farmers registered disapproval with the federal government's decision to remove oats from the
Private Members' Business
marketing activities of the Canadian Wheat Board. Fully 35 per cent of respondents indicate that they strongly disapprove of this decision. This degree of strong disapproval indicates an intensity of opinion on this particular issue and an unlikelihood of farmers changing their opinion with regard to the government action". Those are fairly strong words, Madam Speaker.
What of oats producers? Let us focus on oat producers. The report states at page 11: "Not surprisingly, further cross tabular analysis reveals that oats farmers, 69 per cent, oppose the government's decision to remove the grain, significantly more than non-oats farmers who were 56 per cent". It is no wonder it did not consult with those groups.
The government could also have consulted with the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board. The advisory committee is a committee that is made up of farmers from across western Canada who were voted to the committee by the permit book holders in western Canada, and they are there to advise the Canadian Wheat Board and the government on matters concerning the Wheat Board. The government chose not to consult with it. In fact, the advisory committee was so upset that it publicly called for the resignation of the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds.
The conclusion is clear. The government did consult, but it consulted with those groups that agreed with its opinion. It did not consult with those groups and those bodies that grow oats, that are concerned with oats, and are concerned with the future of the Canadian Wheat Board. Those groups were not consulted or, if they were consulted, they were ignored because they disagreed with the government's position.
The government also said that there were niche markets that the board could not meet. In fact, this was put in a letter to one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Mackenzie, by the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds on April 13, 1989. I will just quote one line where he states that, "the private trade has the flexibility to pursue these specialty markets which command price premiums, as well as to handle bulk sales of feed oats. This will give producers a viable, price sensitive, alternative crop. The new system will provide increased opportunities for oats processing facilities on the Prairies".

Private Members' Business
Since oats was removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, the price has plummeted. There have been morbid conditions, that is admitted, but the price has plummeted. There is no indication at all that the privatization or the removal of oats from the Canadian Wheat Board had any effect whatsoever other than to cause oats to go down.
There are certainly no new oat facilities on the Prairies to process oats. That is not happening. In fact, I have been advised by people in the Wheat Board that they had made a request to the government before the government made this announcement, to allow them to move into the so-called niche markets. They had made that request. They had a plan in place and they could have handled it. The simple fact is that the government chose to simply ignore this request.
Why did the government remove oats from the Canadian Wheat Board? It is very simple and very clear. This is a government that is controlled by the corporate agenda in the country. When it comes to agriculture, it is controlled by the corporate agri-business agenda in the country. Companies like Cargill do not like the Wheat Board. Cargill is a huge private corporation involved in many facets of agri-business. In fact, with respect to grain, it actually markets virtually as much grain as the Canadian Wheat Board does, plus operates all its other areas. It would like to see the Wheat Board weakened or gone. It is pursuing that agenda and has been successful. It is Cargill and others like them who have called for and received this action from the government.
While the government consulted with agri-business on this decision, there was no consideration for farming families. There was no consideration for rural communities. There was no consideration for the beneficial role that the Canadian Wheat Board has played in the development and the growth of western Canada. Rather, private agri-business has spoken and the government has once again displayed its so-called neo-conservatism philosophy and ideology.
The Canadian Wheat Board is self-financing. It functions for farmers. The government is always talking about free enterprise and having people determine their own future. If it really believed that, it would allow farmers to determine the future of the Canadian Wheat Board because the Wheat Board is paid for by farmers
and financed by farmers. They should have the right to decide its future. If the government really believed in people determining their own future, it would allow the Wheat Board to do just that. It would allow farmers and producers to make those decisions.
We need institutions like the Wheat Board because we need the stability in western Canada. Lord knows, times are very difficult in western Canada and times are very unstable. The Canadian Wheat Board provides that stability.
This bill is non-votable. Its only possible purpose is to point out the error of the government and to encourage Canadians to call for a change in its approach, in its philosophy, and in its agenda. Included in its agenda, government should be returning oats to the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and undertaking not to change the Canadian Wheat Board Act with respect to oats, wheat or barley until it properly consults with the users of the Canadian Wheat Board. That includes expanding the Canadian Wheat Board.
In conclusion, I know that I am speaking on behalf of a substantial majority of western Canadians. It is very clear. I simply pray that the government is listening.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after careful consideration of the unique market potential for Canadian oats and in consideration of how that market can best be served, a decision was made to have the industry market oats.
The hon. member opposite has called for a reversal of this decision. He does not seem to believe that the successful marketing of oats into niche markets can best be achieved by having the industry market oats. His proposal would move the industry backward instead of continuing its forward strides.
The government has faith in the abilities of Canadian farmers, including those in the oats industry. We are committed to helping farmers get the highest possible return for their produce and efforts. In keeping with this commitment, the government decided that oats marketing could best be handled by the industry.
We have seen positive developments in the industry that would likely not have happened under the old system. Here are some examples.

Quaker Oats is spending $13 million to modernize and expand its facility in Peterborough, Ontario.
New oats-processing plants are being built. There are the Can-Oat Milling facility located in Portage la Prairie, Manitoba and the Westglen/Agro Company of Canada venture, near my riding in Barrhead, Alberta. At the joint venture announcement last December, Dr. Elugh Homer, the president, stated: "The announcement in 1989 by the Hon. Charles Mayer, that oats would be removed from the Canadian Wheat Board's umbrella was a monumental step in the marketing of oats for Canada and a dominant factor in our decision to locate our new facility in Alberta." These ventures present opportunities both for oats farmers and for rural communities, for example, by way of new job creation.
Other companies such as United Grain Growers and Cargill Limited are responding to the growing demand for high quality oats by setting higher standards to meet market demands. They are rewarding producers of high quality oats with premium prices.
These are opportunities farmers would not have had if the proposal we are discussing today had been in place. Can-Oats has indicated in a letter to my colleague, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, that, as is the case for the plant in Alberta, it was in large part due to the decision on oats that they decided to build their Portage la Prairie plant.
The proposed bill is flawed in some of its basic assumptions. The member sponsoring this bill seems to believe that putting oats under the Canadian Wheat Board by statute would mean they could never be removed from the board's jurisdiction. He is wrong. Parliament could always vote to rescind such legislation. Passing this bill would only hobble the federal government's ability to respond quickly and effectively to changing market conditions. Farmers would just have to adapt to unfavourable conditions while Parliament goes through the long debates necessary to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
Had oats remained under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board, as this bill proposes, and had this government not had the foresight and understanding of the agriculture industry to ensure a market responsive process for selling oats, we would not be seeing processing
Private Members' Business
plants built in rural Canada, such as the one in Barrhead, Alberta. We would not be seeing farmers getting paid a premium for their high quality oats. More processing plants could be built in other rural communities.
That will not happen if we move backward and reverse the decision to allow the industry to market oats. That would tie the hands of those most directly affected. For example, during my recent constituency tour, some farmers, although very happy with crops, were disappointed at the prices and asked me why they could not market their own grain themselves, such as oats. They felt confident that they could sell it if given that opportunity.
I am confident that none of the members here today want to see such opportunities lost for rural communities, such as those in the Wetaskiwin constituency. I do not think anyone wants to see the potential for further growth of the industry nipped in the bud by a narrow and unreasonable view of the future of oats.
In allowing the industry to market oats, the government was confident that the farmers who grow oats and the processors who sell oats would act swiftly to take full advantage of new opportunities. An oats producer association has been formed in Alberta as producers acted for both their own and for the industry's best interests. These producers have demonstrated that they are willing and able to undertake the work of guiding and shaping a healthy oats industry.
Oats producers and Canadian grain traders have demonstrated that they are the ones who can best sell into niche markets. The Canadian Wheat Board has demonstrated its ability to market wheat and barley in the best interests of Canadian farmers on the international markets. Oats are a niche product. Oat export volumes and revenues are small in comparison to wheat and barley. They accounted for only 1.2 per cent of the total value of wheat marketing by the Wheat Board in 1986-87. Oats are more directly affected by changes in the international market, so they require the close attention of those most directly involved in production. By allowing the industry to market oats, this government freed oats producers and traders to undertake a concerted and successful drive to market Canadian oats. Our farmers have been aggressive and successful in their efforts to market Canadian oats. Would the hon. mem-

Private Members' Business
ber see his farming constituents' income reduced? I think not. And yet, his bill could have this effect.
Part of the success of letting industry handle oats marketing relates to the benefits of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement. The U.S. provides producers with a ready market for their product. Industry recognizes the possibilities. They are acting quickly to take advantage of the agreement that benefits Canadian farmers, because they now have the markets and the industrial support to make inroads into the U.S.
As pointed out by Can Oats, the Canada-U.S. trade agreement created an attractive and competitive environment for business by eliminating trade barriers between the two countries. This freedom to move into the marketplace helps oats farmers to maximize their sales and farm income. Oats producers now have new options available to them. These options enable producers to make the decisions that are best for them, decisions that are good for their own farms and for the health of the industry.
Let me give another example. The Oatman, a company started six years ago by Mr. Dennis Lank of Ponoka, began expanding two years ago into the United States and now into other parts of Canada. The Oatman is strictly in the horse industry and now continues to succeed and is planning to expand even further. With direct access to markets, oats producers now share the same benefit as other open market producers such as canola or other off-board grains. By watching cash and futures markets, talking to their local elevator manager and reading market publications, farmers have the price information they need, like those who deal directly and privately with the Oatman.
The federal government has a duty to help farmers develop this industry. Government must not take away the right and opportunity for farmers to decide for themselves how their industry should work. Consequently, Madam Speaker, I cannot support this bill.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I support the principle of this bill. The principle of this private member's bill makes a lot of sense. I think my hon. friend, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, stated the case very well. I would not want to go over much of the ground already covered by my hon.
friend, but there are a number of things that I want to say about this bill and I might even, if I dare, draw on some of the rather cataclysmic events that have been evident on the Hill in the past few hours.
It seems that one of the basic lessons for all politicians and certainly for politicians in government is that you listen to the people. If this government had listened to the agricultural community many months ago in the spring, there would have been no need for this private member's bill, none whatsoever. We would not be discussing this private member's bill if the government had listened, if the government had not removed oats from the Canadian Wheat Board in the first place.
If the government had listened to the agricultural community, we would not be carrying on with this discussion today, but this government does not listen. It does not listen. For example, as my friend, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, said a few moments ago, 63 per cent of farmers surveyed did not want oats taken away from the Canadian Wheat Board, but this government went ahead and did so because it did not listen, it did not consult. In fact, that very same survey indicated that as few as 18 per cent of farmers who were surveyed felt that they were properly and adequately consulted by this government, specifically the minister responsible for grains and oilseeds. I think that is a pretty shabby record. We talk about reputable organizations like the prairie pools, the National Farmers Union, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Advisory Board to the Canadian Wheat Board. They all said this was bad, this would be a bad practice, that the government would regret, that it would rue the day doing this. But the government did not listen. It did not listen.
My hon. friend from Wetaskiwin said a few minutes ago that by returning oats to the Canadian Wheat Board and giving it the protection of statute, it would not stop this government or any future government to take oats away from the Canadian Wheat Board. Well, that is true. We know it is true. But I will tell you one thing. It would not allow the government to be so arbitrary. This government is inclined to be arbitrary, inclined not to consult, not to listen to the people of Canada.
October 5, 1990

I could touch on many subjects. It is not just taking oats away from the Canadian Wheat Board. I can go through a long list of subjects where the government has demonstrated over and over again: " It is our way or no way. We will not listen. We have an agenda and we are going to follow that agenda, and we do not give a darn." That is typical of this government.
If you go back a few months, what was the farming community saying to this government about interest-free cash advances? That program had been around for more than two decades and it had been palpably successful, demonstrably successful. The government did not listen. The government did not consult. It went ahead and said no, that it was cutting it. This was a marvellous program and in a relative sense, was a cheap program, about $25 million, but the goverrtment went right ahead and bulled its way through.
So where are we today? The farm community is going into a deepening crisis, further and further into a crisis, and now we are back to that issue of interest-free cash advances. Major organizations are saying they need it back.
I listened to a spokesperson, one of the parliamentary secretaries, this morning in Question Period. He indicated that there would be some announcement on interest-free cash advances. We hope that it is going to be a positive response and a positive answer. But again the basic lesson is to listen to the people.
I want to raise another matter that is related to this. That is high interest rates, particularly as they apply to western Canada and the agricultural community right across this country. High interest rates have been punishing. They have crucified the farmer. Yet the government ignores. Just this week we had the Economic Council of Canada saying that this government's monetary policy is not working. High interest rates are not working. But you do not sacrifice farmers anywhere in this country for the sake of taking some heat out of the economy in southern Ontario, in metro Toronto, for example. It is not the way to do it.
The government has been told this over and over again, but it will not listen.
Along the same theme the government has been told about the GST and farmers as consumers will pay the
Private Members' Business
GST, despite the fact of millions of petitions, telephone calls, and letters. Millions and millions of people have spoken out. The government is absolutely intransigent, absolutely stubborn on the point. It will not budge.
That brings me to the current events on this Hill. Why do you think that we have this debacle on the Hill. Why do you think what is happening is happening over in the other place? It is because we have a government that is intent upon pushing people beyond their limits.
People can take only so much, and then they reach their breaking point. That is where we are in this country today. It is not normal for hon. senators to stay up all night. They normally go to bed. It is not normal for them to go through some of the strange things that they have the last few hours, but they have been pushed to the wall.
We have been pushed to the wall in this House. Groups have been pushed to the wall. All Canadians have been pushed to the wall, because this government is absolutely bloody-minded. It takes the simplistic notion: "We won the election. We have the numbers, and because we have the numbers we can do anything."
I will tell you, Madam Speaker, that if every Canadian took that attitude, this country would be in chaos. I can tell you about major corporations. They own all the equity. They own all the shares, and they are the bosses. The shareholders are the bosses, but if they do not operate with consensus, if they do not have their workers with them, if there is no mutual respect, if there is no fairness, there will be a breakdown. This government will not understand that. That is why we are where we are today.
I would say in my few moments left that on this issue of the oats being where they ought to be, with the Canadian Wheat Board, the government should listen. There are all kinds of problems. Bankruptcies have gone up sharply in the last few months, and the government better listen.
The debt problem which has been in existence now in a very serious way for about 15 years, and it is getting worse, is something the government is going to have to address very seriously. It cannot just follow its internal agenda as if nobody else counts.

Private Members' Business
I support this bill. It is good in principle, and it is too bad that we could not vote on it.

speechtext:
Now, there is somebody who would not sell something when there is a market available.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville would like to enter into the debate. I invite him to come forward, to take his seat and to sit down.
It is about an issue that has some impact on Saskatchewan. It might be worthy of the hon. member to pay note to it. It deals with oats.
The reason I so seriously want to enter into this debate is that while oats are grown in every region of Canada, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, the hon. member for Macleod and myself, who are in this Chamber, can claim that we come from the oats province.
The province of Alberta is the largest producer of oats anywhere in Canada. We produce about 40 per cent plus of the oats.
This issue impacts very much on the hon. member for Wetaskiwin and the hon. member for Peace River. The major oat growers are in those two constituencies of that province. The fact of the matter is that of the cereal grains in our country only about 5 per cent have traditionally been oats in the last 15 years. Some 90 per cent of the oats the oats that were grown were consumed for feed and another 5 per cent was used for seed, so only 5 per cent of the oats was being marketed.
Anybody who does even a rudimentary analysis of the Canadian Wheat Board and how it operates and works clearly recognizes that put in place there is an agency that is best suited for selling massive volumes of grain particularly into export markets. It does it by shiploads and by large contracts, usually dealing in multiple millions and often into the billions of dollar contracts. Most of our contracts with the Soviet Union are in the neighbourhood of $5 billion. That is not what is happening to the oats industry.
The oats industry for some 15 years now has been an industry that markets largely to the race horse industry in the United States. It sells in 25 to 100 pound bags and into truckload lots. It leaves from the farm gate and heads to specific sources located in another country. More recently, in this past decade, there has been an upsurge of interest in oats as a health food.
What we have, as was correctly described by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, is niche markets, small selective markets. That is not what the Canadian Wheat Board was best able to advantage the farmers to move into. He cites and lays before the House of Commons his evidence that says that farmers were opposed to this.
I recognize that taken in the over all there was an opinion from farmers all across the prairies that somehow this might be weakening the Canadian Wheat Board. But when we take a look at who were the farmers that grew the oats as a industry for export, it was those very farmers who came to government and said: "We request that we have the privilege and the opportunity to
October 5, 1990

create our own market, because the Canadian Wheat Board is not opening up the markets for us and is not doing it in significant enough volumes".
It was because of the growers who grew for an industry, who grew for export, and whose business it was to be in the oats industry that the government responded and met that market. Then came the argument from the hon. member that he can now demonstrate that we can see the results of this move of folly undertaken by the government because the prices are low. It used to be higher. The Canadian Wheat Board dealt with it. The prices are low now, therefore there is a connection.
How convenient it was that he also forgot to add the enormity of the surplus of the feed grains in every grain growing region of the world and that it is not the case of the marketing situation. It would not matter if the Canadian Wheat Board was marketing it now. When you have enormous surpluses around the world in feed grains, obviously you are going to have a decrease in price. It is not a change in the marketing system that has impacted on price. It is intellectually wrong to try and draw that connection and to lay it before people as if somehow there is a connection between the two.

I want to hitchhike on that bit of shouting from across the way. The hon. member says that the prices went up. I very much believe that that is the pressure and that will be the absolute result of being able to self-market in a small percentage of an industry where you have the opportunity to find those markets and to hit the foods.
There are three major plants in Canada that are expanding: two in Ontario and one in Alberta. They are spending multiples of millions of dollars to build new oat facilities, signalling the fact that there is a new confidence in the oat industry after years and years of decline in oat processing in this country. We then change the process and, within the year, three new plants spend multiples of millions of dollars to make the oat industry expand.
I have no qualm with any argument saying that the prices are going up. What my hon. colleague from Wetaskiwin said precisely was that high quality oat prices are going up. That market is being met. It is only the
Private Members' Business
lower grade qualities that are lacking in price of any substantive amount and that is because there is a surplus of feed grains in the market.
I would like to come back to the other allegation that was made by hon. members opposite, that in the consulting process the Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba wheat pools were not consulted. The truth of the matter is that I have not seen much more enthusiasm for the opportunity to market oats than there was by the agency called Excel in Calgary. It said it could meet the market, find the niches, put oats in and, given the long haul, it would advantage farmers in a very significant way. Excel is an agency of the Alberta Wheat Pool.
In speaking at the time that this move was made, I was told by officials of the Alberta Wheat Pool that they would take a public face against this. At the same time one of their agencies was telling me that it was quite enthusiastically looking forward to marketing oats. It believed that there was an opportunity for a broadening of the market and that more farmers would be able to grow oats because they would be able to market more oats than the present system was able to do.
Where do we come back to when we come full circle on this argument? This is not a question of, as I think the NDP is trying to impute upon the government, an intent to weaken the Canadian Wheat Board. That is not the view of the Government of Canada. We believe in the Canadian Wheat Board. We believe it is doing a good job. We have taken a single commodity that represented 2 per cent of the total marketing capacity which was not being marketed adequately and have said that there is a better approach. It is going to demonstrate itself that it will be a better approach. That being done, advantaging farmers, the NDP has not recognized that the Wheat Board markets better to the larger volumes on the international scale. This is a niche market aimed at a racehorse industry, farm to farm, farm to farm, or from farm to processor to the food industry in the specialized rolled oat industry.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-230 standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.

October 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
This bill goes back to the spring of 1989 when the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds unilaterally announced that he was taking the marketing of oats from under the arm of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is interesting that this government which used to talk a great deal about consulting with Canadians did precious little if any consultation with Canadian farmers in western Canada when he took this action.
It seems that he consulted with the Canadian wheat growers, the barley growers, the canola growers, the hog and beef producers, but for some reason or other he did not take any time to consult with oat growers. If he had consulted with some of the big farm organizations like the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the Prairie Pools Incorporated, which have something like 130 farm members, he would have found out that the farmers did not want oats removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw is proposing to put this back under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is very interesting that hon. members who spoke this afternoon from the government side suggested that somehow the hon. member was not making the presentation in a very fair way.
The Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee had its district meeting in the spring of 1989. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin who spoke this afternoon was saying that this was a great thing. If the hon. member for Wetaskiwin had taken time to attend that meeting in the spring of 1989, he would have found that 82 farmers showed up at the Wetaskiwin meeting-I assume he did not himself-and that a motion was put to reinstate oats under the Canadian Wheat Board and it passed 53 to 8. If he attended that same meeting in his own home town, he would have known that a motion was passed to remove the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds. They called on the Prime Minister to take that action and that was passed, likewise, by a vote of 36 to 21.
The hon. member for Crowfoot would know, if he had taken the time to analyse the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee meetings, that similar meetings calling not only for the reinstatement of oats to the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, and in many
cases calling for the removal of the minister responsible for grains and oilseeds were held in Stettler, in Westlock, in La Crete, in Spirit River, and in Valleyview. Then he would not be opposing this motion which is before the House today.
If we look at what has happened to oat prices since the minister's announcement, we could hardly get a more dramatic telling of a tale. I believe the announcement came some time in January 1989, and the top price for oats at that time was $156 a tonne. Today, in October 1990, only some 18 months later, that price has dropped to $109 a tonne. We can see that removing oats from the Wheat Board may have done something for those producers that the minister consulted with, most of them not oat producers but barley producers, wheat producers, canola producers and others that he claims to have consulted with, and perhaps some of the livestock groups. It really has not done much for securing new niche markets or ensuring the stability of the industry. In fact it has gone down very dramatically.
What we face today is a government that is determined, through free trade and through supporting and assisting large grain marketing agencies, to try to break orderly marketing in this country. Unfortunately, it is doing too good a job in my opinion. Removing oats is the first step. Barley will likely be next. Ultimately, if it was around long enough which I do not believe it will be, it would eventually disband the Canadian Wheat Board.
Clearly, if we meet privately with the representatives of the Saskatchewan Pool, the Alberta Pool or Manitoba Pool, they will tell us that as the borders are opened up under that free trade deal the power and the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board is going to be severely tested.
I believe that two things happened in the spring of 1989. It is hard to tell which one was the most harmful but removing oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board was very harmful. Equally harmful was the budget of the great and powerful Michael Wilson because in that budget, in the spring of 1989, he removed one-half billion dollars of support to Canadian agriculture, everything from dairy support programs, to crop insurance, to prairie agriculture rehabilitation of branch lines, to the advance payment program, to the at and east program, to a whole broad range.

What we have as our negotiators sit down at GATT this fall in Geneva is a Canadian agriculture industry which is on its knees praying, not negotiating from a position of strength like the United States or the European Economic Community negotiators, that they will get some kind of a deal out of the GATT negotiations. The reason they are in that position is because the government has totally disarmed them to fight the subsidy war. They come to the negotiating table with no armaments. It would be like sending our ships off to the Persian Gulf without the proper armaments, without the proper military equipment. That is the position our negotiators are in.
This fall farmers growing wheat in western Canada can deliver something like three bushels per acre. That amounts to about $12 best. That is No. 1 wheat. How can a farmer spending $70 or $80 an acre to put in a crop survive? He cannot. So we go to that table having to make a deal.
Last fall, for three or four months we pleaded with the Minister of Agriculture not to take away the interest-free cash advances. It is a very inexpensive program for the Government of Canada, something like $25 million or $27 million. It provides in the short term, six to nine months, something like $400 million or $500 million of cash flow. It increases the value of the crop. It gives the farmer flexibility. They would not do it.
Everybody opposed it, with the exception perhaps of the western Canadian wheat growers, who now have reversed their position and even they oppose it. The farmer has absolutely no cash flow this fall. What will happen, nobody knows. Hopefully the Minister of Agriculture will come to his senses and reinstate it at least for this year. It will not be enough. It might be only half a billion dollars but it will provide some cash flow.
Those actions by the government have put our negotiators at GATT in a very weak position. We are moving away from orderly marketing. This bill moves us back towards orderly marketing. Therefore, I hope that at the end of the day the government might consider supporting it.

Madam Speaker, it gives me pleasure to rise and support my colleague from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and the other
Private Members' Business
members who have spoken eloquently in support of this bill. I think it is a veiy well thought out and timely bill that he has presented, and one that I think all sectors of the farm community would like to see us move on.
What particularly struck me though were the interventions from the government side of the House in defence of the really indefensible action of taking oats out of the Wheat Board in the arbitrary fashion that it did a year and a half ago. Their defence, I think, indicates quite clearly to everybody why this party, the political party that used to represent the public opinion of half the people on the prairies has now been reduced to a rump on the prairies, the fourth place party on the prairies and sinking even lower. They have lost touch, they do not consult, they do not have any respect for the traditional institutions of the prairies, they are letting their traditional support from the farm community whither away.
Farmers are falling like flies, but because a few of their friends are becoming millionaires, they are saying that everything is a success.
So as to allow the members here to be able to vote on this bill, not talk out the clock, I would like to sum up my remarks and ask the government to allow a vote on this issue.

Madam Speaker, I wonder as a question of clarification how much time do I really have to speak-two minutes?
I would like to clarify a couple of points that were brought up earlier. It is pretty clear to me, and I think to most knowledgeable observers here today, that the debate is really not about whether or not the Canadian Wheat Board is good or bad. I think we all agree that the Canadian Wheat Board has a very important role and maintains a very important place in the marketing of prairie agricultural products.
But I think it is important to point out that oats was causing trouble for the Wheat Board itself. It cost the Canadian Wheat Board a tremendous amount to handle most of the small orders that were being placed for oats. Most of the oat growers are small specialized growers and the transaction costs of the Wheat Board handling these orders was tremendous. Also, it applied cost to all the activities of the Wheat Board.
